facts.text: La Puebla was founded in the late 1600s as a Spanish colonial farming community that built acequias—gravity‑fed irrigation ditches—to turn dry high‑desert land into productive fields.
Acequias in La Puebla not only irrigate crops but also act as social hubs, fostering mutual aid and environmental stewardship amid drought.
La Puebla sits next to Chimayó, sharing an acequia network that links the two villages and supports regional agriculture.
After Mexican independence, land grants continued to encourage settlement, with families extending acequias from the Santa Cruz River to irrigate new plots.
Post‑World War II, the High Road to Taos drew visitors to Chimayó’s Santuario, boosting tourism in La Puebla and surrounding villages.
By the early 1950s, rural electrification reached La Puebla, enabling modern amenities and supporting small‑scale weaving industries.
